svg.title: The toolbox checks the test really failed first, instead of taking anyone's word for it: An assistant runs its tasks through one entry point that keeps each task's own verdict
svg.text: The toolbox checks the test really failed first, instead
of taking anyone's word for it
Scenario: An assistant runs its tasks through one entry point that keeps each task's own verdict
One entry point, the task's own exit code
Nothing typed after the run can change its verdict

g.text: Given a project has a unit test task, one test still waiting for its
code and one test that never ends
A developer's project, as git sees it. project/Taskfile.yml gains a task of its own,
project:test:unit, which hands its arguments to Node's built-in test runner.
Two tests come with it. greeting.test.js expects "Hello, Lambda" from src/greeting.js, which
still returns nothing: the code is not written yet. service.test.js waits an hour for an
answer that never comes.
When the assistant runs a passing check through the runner, and the status file and the
shell both say 0
The assistant hands the task to task devsecops:agent:run, with -x so the task's exit code comes through. The runner
starts it from the root of the repository and sends everything it prints to a log of its own, under tmp/agent-runs.
Then it prints the status file of the run: the task, "state: finished", "exit_code: 0" and the path of the log. The
shell agrees, exit code 0, and the log holds the check's own words, "Nothing in this change switches a check off."

text.tspan: task -x devsecops:agent:run -- devsecops:test:check:no-cheat BASE=HEAD; echo "exit code $?"; cat

g.text: Then the expected RED comes back with the test's own exit code, 1
Same runner, now the expected RED: the greeting test, which fails until the code is written. Node's test runner exits
with 1, and that 1 comes back as it is, in the status file and in the shell.
The log says why: the test "greets the developer by name" expected 'Hello, Lambda' and got ''. Both of Task's "Failed to
run task" lines carry the same exit status 1.

text.tspan: task -x devsecops:agent:run -- project:test:unit -- project/tests/unit/greeting.test.js; echo "exit code $?"; cat

g.text: Then a refused check stays 1 in the status file, even when a pipe hands the shell a 0
The assistant switches the greeting test off: test.skip, on line 5. The same check now refuses the change, and the line
ends in a pipe into tail, the habit that used to hide failures.
The shell prints exit code 0, the exit code of tail. The status file of the run, printed last, still says "exit_code:
1": the pipe changed what the shell saw, not the verdict.

text.tspan: devsecops:test:check:no-cheat BASE=HEAD | tail -n 2; echo "exit code $?"; cat tmp/agent-runs/latest/status

g.text: Then a test that never ends is stopped at the time limit and comes back 124, never 0
The last test never ends. With the time limit set to 3 seconds, the runner stops it and says so: "state: timed-out" and
"exit_code: 124". The shell sees 124 too, never 0.
The last lines come from the log of the run: Node's test runner reports service.test.js "Interrupted while running".
Off camera, the status file is read while the test still runs. It says "state: running" with no exit code: a run that
never comes back never reads as a success.

text.tspan: project/tests/unit/service.test.js; echo "exit code $?"; grep -A2 "Interrupted while running"

● Given: stage ● When: actions ● Then: proofs
